item.title: JLR Forecast
item.description:
One-off briefing on Jaguar Land Rover’s 2026 performance and five-year outlook

Jaguar Land Rover restored production in 2026, but retail sales fell in its latest reported quarter and management expects cash to keep flowing out this financial year. This review looks at what the electric Range Rovers and the reinvented Jaguar offer buyers, what redundancies and retraining mean for employees, and what would make a sustained recovery credible by 2031.

How far has the business recovered?

JLR’s financial year ended on 31 March 2026, so its annual results are not a calendar-year total. Revenue fell 20.9% to £22.9bn and JLR recorded a £244m after-tax loss. The 2025 cyberattack and production stoppage, US tariffs, weaker demand in China and the planned withdrawal of older Jaguars weighed on the year. The January to March quarter was profitable as production recovered, but a fire at a major supplier disrupted output again in spring. See JLR’s full-year results and June-quarter results.

In the latest reported quarter, July to September, revenue rose 20.3% to £5.9bn against a cyber-disrupted comparison period, while retail sales fell from about 85,400 to 79,000 vehicles. JLR reported a £6m profit before tax and exceptional items, but a £451m loss after tax. Exceptional charges included redundancy costs and asset write-downs. For the year ending in March 2027, management lowered its adjusted operating margin guidance to 2–3% and expects about £1.25bn in free cash outflow. See JLR’s September-quarter results, its retail and wholesale update and The Guardian’s results coverage.

What changes for buyers?

Range Rover is adding electric models alongside existing powertrain choices, while Jaguar is repositioning as an all-electric luxury brand. The September launch prices were £109,810 for the Range Rover Sport Electric and £154,070 for the flagship Range Rover Electric, with first deliveries expected in early 2027. Jaguar unveiled the Type 01 in New York in October at an announced starting price of £130,000, with initial deliveries expected in the second half of 2027. See the manufacturer announcements for the Range Rover Electric, Sport Electric and Jaguar Type 01.

Land Rover ranked tenth of 30 brands for overall owner satisfaction, but 23rd for quality and reliability, in the 2026 Auto Express Driver Power survey. The survey reflects existing owners’ experiences, not the reliability of the new electric models.

Where does that leave employees?

JLR announced plans in September to cut about 4,000 roles globally over two years. On 13 November, ITV News reported that around 3,000 staff had agreed to voluntary redundancy, with most expected to leave by the end of November. Agreements are not the same as completed departures. Unite said the plans primarily affected salaried grades and called for greater clarity and action to avoid job losses. See ITV News’s November update and Unite’s September statement.

JLR says it has trained about 10,500 West Midlands employees in electrification. It plans to build the Range Rover GT and a new electric Defender at Halewood in Merseyside. These are commitments to skills and production, not forecasts of net job creation. See JLR’s training figures and November product update.

What would a durable recovery look like?

Management is targeting double-digit revenue growth over five years and wants to reduce the annual volume needed to break even on cash towards 300,000 vehicles. It plans to offer more hybrid and electric options and prioritise North America. The US accounted for about a third of September-quarter wholesales, leaving tariff exposure material. Talks with Stellantis about US product development are non-binding. In China, where JLR retail sales have weakened, its joint venture with Chery began producing the first revived Freelander in July. See JLR’s Investor Day presentation, Stellantis’s statement and JLR’s August update.

The outlook is conditional. In 2027, watch whether deliveries arrive on schedule and whether customers buy at prices close to those announced. In 2028–29, lower costs and sustained positive free cash flow would strengthen the case for recovery. By 2031, the test is whether JLR can fund continued investment while protecting product quality and retaining key skills. The available evidence does not support a precise forecast for individual models or sites.

Sources

  • Jaguar Land Rover, Annual Report 2026 and full-year results, 14 May 2026; June-quarter results, 13 August 2026; and September-quarter results, 13 November 2026. Accounts, operating results and management guidance.
  • Jaguar Land Rover, Investor Day presentation, 17 June 2026, and September-quarter wholesale and retail sales update, October 2026. The presentation sets out targets; the sales update distinguishes shipments to retailers from sales to customers.
  • Jasper Jolly, The Guardian, Jaguar Land Rover reports £451m quarterly loss after cutting 4,000 jobs, 13 November 2026. The 4,000 figure refers to the overall reduction plan, not confirmed departures on that date.
  • Range Rover, Range Rover Electric: A New Era for the Original Luxury SUV, 2 September 2026, and Range Rover Sport Electric: Tuned for Visceral Dynamism, 30 September 2026; Jaguar, Type 01 New York world premiere, published 7 October 2026. Manufacturer sources for launch prices, delivery expectations and training figures.
  • Steve Walker, Auto Express, Range Rover reliability a key focus as brand maps its EV future, 5 November 2026. Includes Driver Power owner-survey results and an interview with Range Rover managing director Martin Limpert.
  • Unite, JLR workers must not pay the price for failings not of their making, 7 September 2026; ITV News, JLR says 3,000 staff already agreed voluntary redundancy under two-year plan, 13 November 2026. Union concerns and the company’s update on voluntary redundancies.
  • Stellantis, Stellantis and JLR to Explore Collaboration Synergies for Product Development in the U.S., 20 May 2026. The announcement describes exploratory talks, not a binding production agreement.

item.title: Pheasant tips
item.description:
One-off briefing on British pheasant and partridge shooting, its history, business and culture

How did an Asian bird become a fixture of the British countryside, and who makes a living from a day’s shooting? This episode traces the pheasant from the old game laws to the modern network of estates, syndicates, suppliers and events. It explains why a bigger bag doesn’t mean more wild birds, weighs the evidence on gamebird releases, and offers practical ways to judge a shoot’s safety and welfare standards and get to know pheasants and partridges through observation. It also looks at what shooting reveals about class, labour and power in Danny the Champion of the World, Out of Africa, The Shooting Party and Gosford Park.

How the pheasant came to look at home

The common pheasant is native to Asia. Finds from Roman Britain have been reported, but early remains do not establish when a continuous population took hold. The British Trust for Ornithology puts the first documented occurrence in medieval times. See BTO BirdFacts: Pheasant and Kristopher Poole’s Bird Introductions.

Gainsborough’s Mr and Mrs Andrews, painted around 1750, links shooting with landownership and income. The Game Act 1831, as enacted, removed the old property qualification for taking game without opening private land to the public. Formal driven shooting spread in the nineteenth century, when an estate’s ability to host a large shoot could signal its owner’s wealth and standing.

Why a bigger bag didn’t mean more wild birds

Historian John Martin treats the early twentieth century as a period of change rather than the simple end of the estate shoot. His work on the post-war period distinguishes the expansion of artificially reared game from the decline of wild partridges associated with changing agricultural practices. A shoot’s tally is not a breeding-population index. See British Game Shooting in Transition, 1900–1945 and BTO BirdFacts: Grey Partridge.

Who gets paid for a day out

Owners can run a shoot themselves, let sporting rights, share costs through a syndicate or sell days commercially. The supply chain can involve game farms, keepers, beaters, pickers-up, contractors, booking platforms, insurers, hospitality providers and game dealers. The historical Savills and Game & Wildlife Conservation Trust Shoot Benchmarking Survey distinguishes quoted prices from realised income; its sample is not a current price guide. GunsOnPegs describes the platform’s role from the operator’s own perspective.

Sporting property and firearms manufacturing are different investments. Beretta Holding’s 2021 acquisition of Holland & Holland is an example of investment in manufacturing, servicing and an established brand. Stable Events’ Game Fair illustrates a separate business built around exhibitors, sponsors, visitors and hospitality.

What the big numbers can’t tell you

Cognisense’s The Value of Shooting 2024, commissioned by 24 rural organisations, estimates £3.3 billion in direct gross value added across UK shooting, not just gamebird shooting. Its £9.3 billion headline is a wider measure, not an additional sum. Neither is a measure of estate profit or a comparison with alternative uses of the land. Defra’s England call for evidence announced a separate independent economic assessment. Research by Tracey Latham-Green, Richard Hazenberg and Simon Denny, published online in Ageing & Society in 2021, examines the social ties and belonging older rural participants found through driven shooting.

Two partridges and two stories about habitat

The grey partridge is native to Britain; the red-legged partridge was introduced from continental Europe. The UK grey partridge breeding index fell 93% between 1967 and 2024, according to BTO BirdFacts. Joah Madden’s 2021 study of UK gamebird releases estimated annual releases of approximately 31.5 million pheasants and 9.1 million red-legged partridges. These are modelled estimates, not a current census.

The jointly funded Natural England and BASC evidence review and a related synthesis distinguish possible habitat benefits from adverse effects associated with releases. Natural England’s 2026 ground-invertebrate review reports reductions in some larger invertebrates in high-density woodland pens, without finding the same result across all settings. Under Defra’s England call for evidence, the government sought evidence on rearing, release and shooting; it was not a proposal to ban game shooting.

What happens to the birds afterwards

Game can reach consumers through dealers, processors, butchers and hospitality businesses. Eat Wild is an advocate for game meat; the Food Standards Agency is the relevant source for food-chain responsibilities and exposure advice.

The fifth-year SHOT-SWITCH report, published in Conservation Evidence in March 2025, found lead shot in approximately 99% of sampled pheasants with recoverable shot from suppliers other than Waitrose in 2024–25. This is a defined retail sample, not a census. The REACH (Amendment) Regulations 2026 provide for separate restrictions in Great Britain, with the main lead-shot transition ending in April 2029.

How to get more out of time in the field

The practical focus is judgement, welfare and unarmed bird observation, rather than firearm technique, hit rates or increasing the bag. Ask organisers who is responsible for safety, how concerns are raised, who responds to injured birds, how the public is accounted for and where the birds go. The sector’s own Code of Good Shooting Practice is a starting point for discussing standards, not proof that a particular operator meets them.

For observation, use the Countryside Code, BTO BirdTrack and BTO species accounts. Don’t touch dead wild birds; follow the official reporting guidance for Great Britain.

From Danny’s filling station to the country house

Roald Dahl’s Danny the Champion of the World (1975) uses pheasant poaching to tell a story about a father and son, class and access to land. It grew from a story published as The Champion of the World in The New Yorker in 1959. Gavin Millar’s 1989 adaptation cast Jeremy Irons and his son Samuel. Isabel Colegate’s The Shooting Party (1980) and Alan Bridges’s film examine competition and restraint at a 1913 estate gathering. Chapter 41 of Thomas Hardy’s Tess of the d’Urbervilles shifts attention to wounded birds after the shooting party has gone.

What the camera chooses to show

Karen Blixen’s Out of Africa (1937), published as Isak Dinesen, concerns colonial Kenya, not British gamebird shooting. Its hunting episodes and account of a shooting accident differ in emphasis from Sydney Pollack’s 1985 adaptation. The American Film Institute catalogue describes the film’s safari encounter; National Museums of Kenya offers a history of the farmhouse beyond Blixen’s time.

Jean Renoir’s The Rules of the Game (1939) uses a hunt to break the rhythm of a country-house comedy. Robert Altman’s Gosford Park (2001) uses a shooting weekend to move between guests and servants. Both repay attention to what the camera makes visible, not only to the conversations of the invited guests.

Back to the November hedge

The history explains how an introduced bird became familiar; it does not establish a particular shoot’s economic, ecological or welfare record. The supplied research did not identify a completed independent economic assessment for Defra’s England review. The most useful follow-up is evidence specific to individual operations and places: who does the work, what has changed in the habitat, how welfare is handled and where the birds go.

Sources

  • Kristopher Poole, Bird Introductions, and BTO BirdFacts: Pheasant give context for the distinction between early finds and a documented population.
  • The National Gallery’s Mr and Mrs Andrews, the Game Act 1831 as enacted and John Martin’s British Game Shooting in Transition, 1900–1945 trace estate culture, access and change.
  • The Savills and Game & Wildlife Conservation Trust Shoot Benchmarking Survey describes a historical sample, not current prices. GunsOnPegs and The Game Fair describe their own commercial services.
  • Cognisense, The Value of Shooting 2024, was commissioned by 24 rural organisations and covers shooting more broadly than pheasant and partridge days.
  • BTO BirdFacts: Grey Partridge records breeding-population change. Joah Madden’s How Many Gamebirds Are Released in the UK Each Year? (2021) estimates releases. These sources measure different things.
  • Natural England and BASC, Ecological Consequences of Gamebird Releasing and Management on Lowland Shoots in England (2020), distinguishes effects of releases from associated management. Related reviews share evidence and should not be counted as independent corroboration.
  • Defra’s England call for evidence ran from 4 September to 1 November 2026. Philip Case’s November 2026 reporting in Farmers Weekly describes the differing views on oversight. The evidence call was not a proposal to ban shooting.
  • Game-meat advocacy: Eat Wild. Evidence on lead: Rhys Green and colleagues’ fifth-year SHOT-SWITCH report, Conservation Evidence, March 2025. The quoted percentage applies to a defined retail sample, not to all gamebirds shot or sold.
  • Practical reading: the industry’s Code of Good Shooting Practice, the Countryside Code, BTO BirdTrack and GOV.UK guidance on reporting dead wild birds.
  • Read and watch: Roald Dahl’s The Champion of the World (1959), the precursor to Danny the Champion of the World; Isabel Colegate’s The Shooting Party (1980); Thomas Hardy’s Tess of the d’Urbervilles, chapter 41; Karen Blixen’s Out of Africa (1937) and Sydney Pollack’s 1985 film; Jean Renoir’s The Rules of the Game (1939); and Robert Altman’s Gosford Park (2001).

item.title: Anthropic public listing
item.description:
One-off briefing on the global market response to Anthropic’s IPO

Anthropic raised a record sum in its initial public offering, yet its shares closed below the offer price by the fourth trading session. This briefing examines the debut alongside a wider market sell-off and compares how investors took part in Japan, Europe and Brazil. It distinguishes demand for the offering from subsequent trading and explains what the company’s financial disclosures can tell investors that the first week’s share prices cannot.

A record sale and a quick reversal

Anthropic priced 980 million shares at $83 each, above its initial range of $70 to $78. The base offering totalled $81.3 billion, overtaking SpaceX’s June record. The gross public offering rose to $93.5 billion after the underwriters took up their option to buy additional shares. That total includes proceeds attributable to selling shareholders and excludes a separate $26 billion private placement. Anthropic’s final prospectus; Nasdaq’s 20 November market review.

The shares opened at $111.50 on 19 November and closed at $97.17, up 17.1% from the offer price. They fell in each of the next three sessions, closing at $81.91 on 24 November. That was 1.3% below the offer price but 26.5% below the first public trade. Reuters, via Euronext; historical prices.

The debut did not lift the wider market

The Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 both fell more than 2% on 19 November despite Anthropic’s debut gain. The S&P 500 fell another 3.7% the following day. In the 20 November Asian sessions, Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 5.06% and Taiwan’s TAIEX fell 6.23%. These moves show that the debut did not coincide with a broad rally; they do not establish that the listing caused the sell-off. The Guardian’s debut coverage; Associated Press, 20 November; Nikkei Indexes; Taiwan Stock Exchange.

Technology analyst Bob O’Donnell told Reuters that the offering offered some reassurance about appetite for AI, but was only a first test. The Guardian reported continuing concern about whether returns on AI investment would justify the spending.

How overseas investors took part

In Japan, the issuer’s Japanese-language pricing notice showed a domestic offer of about 36.1 million shares, worth roughly $3 billion. Reuters, citing two people familiar with the offering, reported that Japanese investors had sought $9.4 billion in shares. The larger figure measures requests, not purchases. Japanese pricing notice.

Bloomberg reported that retail investors across the UK and continental Europe received about $1.1 billion in shares. That regional allocation is not a measure of total orders or a country-by-country breakdown. Bloomberg’s European retail allocation report.

In Brazil, São Paulo exchange B3 launched a real-denominated depositary receipt on the day of the Nasdaq debut. B3 reported R$460.2 million in first-day turnover, more than three times the equivalent SpaceX receipt’s debut turnover. This was local trading in a product linked to the US shares, not a Brazilian IPO allocation. B3’s Portuguese-language turnover report.

What the first week could not settle

Anthropic reported $17 billion in revenue for the September 2026 quarter, up from $1.4 billion a year earlier, and a $567 million operating loss. Its prospectus disclosed $900.9 billion in purchase and lease commitments, predominantly for computing and infrastructure. Those commitments extend over years and are not a current debt balance. The prospectus also says up to 303 million additional shares become eligible for sale on 15 December, subject to applicable restrictions; eligibility does not mean they will be sold. Anthropic’s final prospectus.

MSCI announced that it would add Anthropic to its global standard indexes at the 30 November close, effective 1 December. Index inclusion and changes in the supply of tradable shares can influence prices without resolving whether revenue growth will translate into durable margins and cash flow. MSCI index announcement.

Sources

US share prices are regular-session figures through 24 November 2026. The first public trade is shown separately from closing prices. The overseas figures measure different things: subscription requests in Japan, retail allocations in Europe and secondary-market turnover in Brazil.

  • Anthropic, final prospectus, Form 424B4, 18 November 2026 — offer terms, financial results, commitments and share-sale restrictions. Nasdaq, Chartstopper: November 20, 2026 — offering totals and market context.
  • The Guardian, Anthropic shares end first day of trading at $97 as Wall Street closes sharply lower, 19 November 2026; Reuters, Anthropic’s blockbuster debut tests Wall Street’s faith in AI boom, 19 November 2026, syndicated by Euronext; and Anthropic historical share prices.
  • Associated Press, S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year, 20 November 2026; Nikkei Indexes daily summary and Taiwan Stock Exchange daily report, both for 20 November 2026.
  • Anthropic, 発行価格等の決定に関するお知らせ, 19 November 2026 — Japanese-language pricing notice hosted by SBI Securities. The subscription figure is from Reuters’ 20 November Tokyo report, which cited two people familiar with the sale.
  • Bloomberg, European Retail Snags $1.1 Billion of Anthropic IPO Stock, 19 November 2026; B3, Negociação do BDR da Anthropic (ANTH34) bate SpaceX e chega a R$ 460,2 milhões em estreia na B3 — Brazilian debut turnover.
  • MSCI, US: Anthropic A, 19 November 2026 — scheduled index inclusion.

item.title: Weather in Scotland
item.description:
One-off briefing on how Scotland’s weather changed from 1926 to 2025

This five-minute scientific report uses long-term records to explain why Scotland can have wetter winters and still face water shortages. It also looks at warming, fewer frost days and declining snow cover at Highland study sites, and separates what has been measured from what climate models project.

Findings and method

The century review covers 1926–2025. It compares averages for 1926–1955 and 1996–2025, rather than fitting a trend across all 100 years. Between those two periods, Scotland’s mean annual temperature rose from 7.15°C to 7.87°C and average annual precipitation rose from about 1,403 to 1,565 millimetres. Winter (December–February) precipitation increased by about 22%, compared with about 2% in summer (June–August). The frost comparison uses different windows: 1931–1960 and 2016–2025. The Highland satellite study measures snow cover at nine sites, not snowfall across Scotland.

Sources

  1. Met Office, HadUK-Grid: Scotland mean air temperature series. Source for the period averages and the national annual mean.
  2. Met Office, HadUK-Grid: Scotland precipitation series. Source for annual, winter and summer rainfall comparisons.
  3. Mike Kendon and colleagues, State of the UK Climate in 2025, International Journal of Climatology, 14 July 2026. Places the Scottish figures in the wider UK record and uses different comparison periods for its rainfall assessment.
  4. Met Office, UK Climate Extremes. Lists the 34.8°C Scottish station record set at Charterhall on 19 July 2022.
  5. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, AR6 Synthesis Report: Summary for Policymakers, 2023. Assesses the evidence for human-caused global warming.
  6. Met Office, Storm Babet, October 2023 event assessment. Documents rainfall totals and flooding at Brechin.
  7. Associated Press, Storm Hits Northern Europe, Killing at Least 4 People, 21 October 2023. Contemporary reporting on the Brechin evacuations.
  8. Scottish Environment Protection Agency, Autumn Water Situation Report 2025. Documents the dry water year in eastern Scotland and contrasts conditions across the country.
  9. World Weather Attribution, Autumn and winter storm rainfall in the UK and Ireland was made about 20% heavier by human-caused climate change, 22 May 2024. The estimate applies to rainfall on stormy days across the study region, not to Storm Babet alone or to wind strength.
  10. Benedict D. Spracklen and Dominick V. Spracklen, Decline of Late Spring and Summer Snow Cover in the Scottish Highlands from 1984 to 2022: A Landsat Time Series, Remote Sensing, 6 April 2023.
  11. Met Office, HadUK-Grid: Scotland air-frost days series.
  12. Adaptation Scotland, Climate Projections for Scotland: Summary, 2025. Summarises projected seasonal changes under different emissions pathways.

item.title: Padel
item.description:
One-off briefing on the rise and economics of padel
One-off briefing on the rise and economics of padel. From a private court in Acapulco to a global booking boom, we look at why this blend of tennis scoring and squash-style rebounds caught on, why court hire drives most of the spending measured, and what Sweden’s experience tells us about building ahead of demand. We also compare Premier Padel with North America’s team league and look at what the world’s top players earn in prize money.
## Sources and research notes
1. **Origins, rules and related sports.** International Padel Federation (FIP), [History](https://www.padelfip.com/history/), for the Corcueras, Marbella, Argentina and the first world championships. See also FIP’s *Rules of Padel* and the Lawn Tennis Association’s *Pickleball rules & scoring* for the comparison between the games.
2. **Global participation.** FIP, [World Padel Report 2026](https://www.padelfip.com/world-padel-report-2026/) and its [14 October 2026 release](https://www.padelfip.com/2026/10/fip-world-padel-report-2026-is-online-more-than-40-million-players-courts-up-by-20-and-a-new-study-on-economic-impact-e8-6-billion-in-gdp/). The 2026 edition estimates more than 40 million active players and more than 91,200 courts. The 2025 edition, released 2 December 2025, put participation above 35 million. Neither estimate is directly comparable to Playtomic’s player count.
3. **Bookings, club revenue and Sweden.** Playtomic and Strategy&, [Global Padel Report 2026](https://8258038.fs1.hubspotusercontent-na1.net/hubfs/8258038/Global%20Padel%20Report/Playtomic%20Global%20Padel%20Report%202026-1.pdf), May 2026. The report estimates 19.4 million players in 2025 under a different methodology from the federation’s. Its monthly booking-revenue benchmarks are €3,531 per court at the upper end of the sample and €736 at the lower end. These are platform-based benchmarks, not industry averages or profit margins. The report also supplies the Swedish court counts.
4. **British participation and the cost of play.** Lawn Tennis Association, *LTA Annual Report and Accounts show growth of tennis and padel in 2025*, 20 May 2026, and its 2026 media guide. The participation figures do not count regular paying customers. BBC, [Padel is exploding across the UK. So why can booking a court cost £100 an hour?](https://news.files.bbci.co.uk/include/newsspec/41093-padel-vj-scrollymation/english/app), 1 August 2026, for court prices and independent reporting on Swedish closures and bankruptcies.
5. **Spending versus GDP.** OpenEconomics, [Impatto economico del padel: 8,6 miliardi di PIL nel 2026](https://www.openeconomics.eu/post/impatto-economico-del-padel-8-6-miliardi-di-pil-nel-2026), and FIP’s 14 October 2026 release describe the same study, not two independent estimates. The model estimates €6.84 billion in spending, of which 67.2% was court hire and 1.4% was professional tournaments. It excludes media rights, sponsorship, coaching and membership fees. The €8.6 billion GDP estimate includes wider effects through supply chains and wage-supported spending; it is not an industry turnover figure.
6. **The tour merger and its commercial partners.** Qatar Sports Investments, [QSI reaches agreement to acquire World Padel Tour](https://www.qsi.com.qa/qsi-reaches-agreement-to-acquire-world-padel-tour/), 24 August 2023; Spain’s National Markets and Competition Commission, *The CNMC authorises with commitments the purchase of World Padel Tour by Qatar Sports Investments*, 27 March 2024; and Premier Padel’s Red Bull partnership announcement, 23 February 2024. The acquisition and partnership announcements describe the arrangements, not the tour’s profitability.
7. **The team-league model.** Rob Schaefer, Sports Business Journal, [Pro Padel League plans changes to player comp, schedule after fund raise](https://www.sportsbusinessjournal.com/Articles/2026/04/08/pro-padel-league-plans-changes-to-player-comp-schedule-after-fund-raise/), 8 April 2026, for the reported US$15 million Series A and the league’s player-compensation plans.
8. **Rankings and prize money.** FIP, [FIP Rankings](https://www.padelfip.com/fip-rankings/), 23 November 2026 snapshot; Kuwait Major draw, October 2026; and Premier Padel men’s and women’s rulebooks, section 8.2. The €48,700 award per winner applies to that event, not necessarily to other tournaments. Joaquín Serna, AS, *¿Cuánto dinero han ganado los mejores jugadores de Premier Padel en 2025?*, 16 December 2025, calculated around €487,000 each in 2025 prize money for Coello and Tapia and €353,000 each for Triay and Brea. These figures do not establish typical player income, take-home pay or the value of endorsements.

item.title: Milburn report
item.description:
Alan Milburn’s 2026 review proposes a stronger route from school into training and work, alongside a benefits redesign that could leave some young people with less cash support. We examine the evidence behind the report, compare reactions from four UK news outlets, and ask what the EU and other G20 economies can teach Britain about youth guarantees and apprenticeships. Then we separate the money Labour has already committed from what Milburn wants it to spend before and beyond the next election.
## The Milburn report: Can Britain build a better route into work?
Approximately 14 minutes. Research cut-off: 23 November 2026. The episode discusses the **final November review**, not just the May interim diagnosis. The review’s roughly 5% participation-gap target, its modelled 6.8% rate and its long-term fiscal projection are separate claims. None is an observed outcome or a government funding commitment.
### The report and the data
1. Alan Milburn, [*From a Welfare State to a Working State: a new settlement for the next generation*](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/from-a-welfare-state-to-a-working-state-a-new-settlement-for-the-next-generation/from-a-welfare-state-to-a-working-state-a-new-settlement-for-the-next-generation), 17 November 2026, and the [analytical annex](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/from-a-welfare-state-to-a-working-state-a-new-settlement-for-the-next-generation/from-a-welfare-state-to-a-working-state-analytical-annex). See the annex for the baseline, employment modelling and fiscal assumptions. 2. Alan Milburn, [*Young people and work: interim report*](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/young-people-and-work-interim-report/young-people-and-work-interim-report), 28 May 2026. 3. Office for National Statistics, [*Young people not in education, employment or training (NEET), UK: August 2026*](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peoplenotinwork/unemployment/bulletins/youngpeoplenotineducationemploymentortrainingneet/august2026), reporting April to June 2026 estimates.
### Press reactions and independent scrutiny
4. The Guardian, [‘The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation’](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/17/the-guardian-view-on-the-milburn-report-a-manifesto-for-youth-participation), and Patrick Butler, ‘Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone’, both 17 November 2026. The editorial and Butler’s analysis are distinct pieces. 5. The Spectator, ‘The Milburn report doesn’t go far enough’, editorial, issue dated 21 November 2026. 6. Lucy Burton, The Telegraph, [‘Burnham opens door to retreat on Rayner’s job reforms’](https://www.aol.com/articles/milburn-attacks-rayner-job-reforms-210337000.html), 17 November 2026. Link is to a syndicated copy, not independent corroboration. 7. Financial Times, *FT News Briefing*, ‘Leak of 15mn Deutsche Bank files exposes systemic failures’, 17 November 2026. Chris Smyth’s youth-policy segment begins roughly nine and a half minutes in. The supplied research used the public episode listing and a third-party transcript, not the paywalled FT article or official transcript. 8. Institute for Fiscal Studies, [‘Milburn Review of Young People and Work: IFS response’](https://ifs.org.uk/articles/milburn-review-young-people-and-work-ifs-response), and Lindsay Judge, Resolution Foundation, ‘Three figures we should all pay attention to in the Milburn Review’, both 17 November 2026.
### International comparisons
9. ILO and OECD, [*Youth at Work in the G20: Progress and Policy Action towards the Antalya Goal*](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/youth-at-work-in-the-g20-progress-and-policy-action-towards-the-antalya-goal_e9552f40-en.html), 2025; G20 education and employment ministers, [Mendoza joint declaration](https://g20.in/en/docs/2018/Education_and_employment_joint_declaration.pdf), 6 September 2018; and G20 Johannesburg Leaders’ Declaration, 22 November 2025, for the Nelson Mandela Bay target. 10. European Commission, [*The reinforced Youth Guarantee*](https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/policies-and-activities/eu-employment-policies/youth-employment-support/reinforced-youth-guarantee_en), adopted in 2020; European Court of Auditors, *Youth unemployment – have EU policies made a difference?*, Special Report No. 5/2017. The audit concerns the earlier guarantee. 11. National vocational comparators: Germany’s dual vocational system, discussed in the OECD’s 2025 work on German apprenticeship support; Australia’s National Skills Agreement and fee-free vocational training; and Brazil’s Ministry of Labour apprenticeship guidance under the *Lei da Aprendizagem*. These examples illustrate policy design rather than comparable estimates of impact. 12. Presidency of South Africa, [*Presidential Youth Employment Intervention quarterly progress report*](https://www.presidency.gov.za/sites/default/files/2025-06/PYEI%20Q4%20Report%202025.pdf), 2025.
### UK investment and decisions to watch
13. UK Government, [‘Major employment drive to help unlock 200,000 new jobs and apprenticeships for next generation’](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/major-employment-drive-to-help-unlock-200000-new-jobs-and-apprenticeships-for-next-generation); Department for Work and Pensions, Jobs Guarantee expansion announcement, 14 November 2026. 14. HM Treasury, [*Budget 2026*](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/budget-2026-document/budget-2026-html), 28 October 2026, for apprenticeship brokerage funding. 15. UK Government, [‘Government commits to new settlement for young people and to invest in success rather than pay for failure’](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/government-commits-to-new-settlement-for-young-people-and-to-invest-in-success-rather-than-pay-for-failure), and Department for Education college funding announcement, 17 November 2026. 16. Office for Budget Responsibility, *Economic and Fiscal Outlook*, October 2026. The OBR indicated it would assess resulting policies once the government’s response and details were clear; the review’s numbers should not be treated as OBR-certified savings. 17. House of Commons Library, [*MPs standing down from the Commons at the next general election*](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10971/), for the latest possible polling date. The Work and Pensions Committee opened its Milburn inquiry on 19 November 2026, with written evidence due on 16 December.
**What to watch:** The White Paper and 2027 Spending Review are the tests of whether plans become funded entitlements. Look for multi-year allocations, published waiting times and sustained outcomes, and transitional protections for young people whose disability-related payments could change.

item.title: Learning science
item.description:
When should a teacher explain, ask a question or let learners try a problem first? This episode outlines four pillars of learning science: prior knowledge, durable memory, feedback and self-regulation, and applying knowledge in new situations. It uses Plato’s geometry dialogue to explain the Socratic method, then compares it with explicit instruction, guided inquiry, productive failure and peer instruction. The focus is on what the evidence can tell us about each approach, and what remains uncertain.
## Learning science: the Socratic method and its alternatives
**Running time:** Approximately 6 minutes. The episode distinguishes three outcomes: remembering material, explaining the reasoning behind it, and applying it independently to a new problem.
### Sources keyed to the master script
1. National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2018), [*How People Learn II: Learners, Contexts, and Cultures*](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/24783). Consensus report on prior knowledge, memory, motivation and self-regulation. 2. US Institute of Education Sciences (2007), [*Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning*](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/Docs/PracticeGuide/20072004.pdf). Practice guide on worked examples, spacing, quizzes and explanatory questions. 3. John Sweller and Graham A. Cooper (1985), [“The Use of Worked Examples as a Substitute for Problem Solving in Learning Algebra”](https://doi.org/10.1207/s1532690xci0201_3), *Cognition and Instruction*. The experiments tested performance on problems sharing the structure of the worked examples. 4. Henry L. Roediger III and Jeffrey D. Karpicke (2006), [“Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention”](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01693.x), *Psychological Science*. Experiments comparing repeated study and retrieval at different test delays. 5. Sterre K. Ruitenburg and colleagues (2026), [“A Meta-Analysis of the Effectiveness and Boundary Conditions of Retrieval Practice, Distributed Practice, and Interleaved Practice in Authentic School Classrooms”](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10648-026-10225-5), *Educational Psychology Review*. Pooled evidence from primary and secondary classrooms. 6. Benedikt Wisniewski, Klaus Zierer and John Hattie (2020), [“The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research”](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6987456/), *Frontiers in Psychology*. The effects of feedback vary with the information it provides. 7. Plato, [*Meno*, sections 82b–85b](https://adfonteslibrary.org/work-plato-meno). Primary text for the square-doubling dialogue. 8. Andrea Paula Goldin and colleagues (2017), [“Producing or reproducing reasoning? Socratic dialog is very effective, but only for a few”](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5363905/), *PLOS ONE*. A small study adapting Plato’s dialogue; it did not compare the dialogue with an alternative lesson. 9. Ard W. Lazonder and Ruth Harmsen (2016), [“Meta-Analysis of Inquiry-Based Learning: Effects of Guidance”](https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315627366), *Review of Educational Research*. A synthesis on the benefits of support during inquiry. 10. Tanmay Sinha and Manu Kapur (2021), [“When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure”](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3102/00346543211019105), *Review of Educational Research*. Compares problem-first and instruction-first sequences. 11. Michelle K. Smith and colleagues (2011), [“Combining Peer Discussion with Instructor Explanation Increases Student Learning from In-Class Concept Questions”](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3046888/), *CBE—Life Sciences Education*. The study measured immediate performance on a related question in two university genetics courses. 12. Education Endowment Foundation, [*Dialogic Teaching* trial](https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/projects-and-evaluation/projects/dialogic-teaching). Includes the 2017 evaluation and 2019 follow-up of a broader classroom-talk programme, not a stand-alone test of the Socratic method. 13. Albert Stumm (30 September 2026), [“Cramming for exams? Experts weigh in on how to study better”](https://apnews.com/article/b42ae895d418351dcfd001747869c21c), Associated Press. Practical reporting on study habits, not an independent test of their effectiveness.

item.title: Quantum physics
item.description:
Send electrons through two slits one at a time and they build up a striped pattern. Record which slit each electron takes and the stripes disappear. Why? This beginner’s guide uses that experiment to explain superposition, uncertainty and entanglement, tracing the ideas from Planck and Einstein to the researchers testing quantum physics today. Along the way, we’ll see how the same theory helps us read starlight, measure gravity with atomic clocks and build quantum computers—and where the evidence still leaves questions open. No equations or prior physics needed.
# Quantum physics: From two slits to the early universe **Estimated listening time:** 10–11 minutes. No prior physics needed.
## What you’ll learn - **Quantisation:** Atoms have specific allowed energies. The gaps between them determine which frequencies of light atoms can emit or absorb. - **Superposition and uncertainty:** Interference shows why quantum alternatives aren’t just ordinary possibilities we happen not to know about. Uncertainty limits how sharply position and momentum can both be specified in the same state. - **Entanglement:** Bell tests rule out local hidden-instruction explanations under the test’s assumptions, but do not enable faster-than-light messages. - **What remains open:** Decoherence helps explain why interference is hard to see in everyday objects, but doesn’t settle the measurement problem. Testing quantum systems in gravity does not establish that gravity itself is quantised. - **What counts as progress:** Improving error correction on quantum hardware is a different benchmark from outperforming a conventional computer on a useful task.
## Sources keyed to the master script ### Foundations and contributors [1] Bach and colleagues, [‘Controlled double-slit electron diffraction’](https://doi.org/10.1088/1367-2630/15/3/033018), *New Journal of Physics* (2013). The original experiment builds up an interference pattern from individual electron hits.
[2] [‘Measurement-induced decoherence and information in double-slit interference’](https://www.nist.gov/publications/measurement-induced-decoherence-and-information-double-slit-interference), *American Journal of Physics* / NIST (2016). Explains the link between physical path information and loss of interference.
[3] [‘The Tumultuous Birth of Quantum Mechanics’](https://physics.aps.org/articles/v18/24), *Physics*, American Physical Society (2025). A history of the theory’s development with links to foundational papers. See also the APS centenary chronology, [‘Celebrating the First Century of Quantum Physics and Preparing for the Next One’](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.150001), *Physical Review Letters* (2025).
[4] [‘October 1925: Einstein and Bose predict Bose-Einstein condensation’](https://www.aps.org/apsnews/2005/10/this-month-in-physics-history), *APS News* (October 2005); and [‘Quantum Milestones, 1928: The Dirac Equation Unifies Quantum Mechanics and Special Relativity’](https://physics.aps.org/articles/v18/20), *Physics*, American Physical Society (2025).
[5] [‘The Relation of Wave and Particle Viewpoints’](https://www.feynmanlectures.caltech.edu/III_02.html), *The Feynman Lectures on Physics*, Vol. III, ch. 2, Caltech. Further reading on the link between a wave packet and the position–momentum uncertainty relation.
[6] Chien-Shiung Wu and colleagues, [‘Experimental Test of Parity Conservation in Beta Decay’](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.105.1413), *Physical Review* (15 February 1957). The original paper on the failure of mirror symmetry in this decay.
### Entanglement and measurement [7] Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen, [‘Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?’](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.47.777), *Physical Review* (15 May 1935).
[8] John Bell, [‘On the Einstein Podolsky Rosen paradox’](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysicsPhysiqueFizika.1.195), *Physics Physique Fizika* (1964); and the Nobel Prize’s [2022 Physics Prize announcement](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2022/press-release/) (4 October 2022), describing the work of Clauser, Aspect and Zeilinger.
[9] Hensen and colleagues, [‘Loophole-free Bell inequality violation using electron spins separated by 1.3 kilometres’](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature15759), *Nature* (21 October 2015). The Delft-led experiment addressed the locality and detection loopholes together; it did not eliminate the need for assumptions about the independence of the measurement settings.
[10] Maximilian Schlosshauer, [‘Decoherence, the measurement problem, and interpretations of quantum mechanics’](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.76.1267), *Reviews of Modern Physics* (2005). A review of what decoherence explains and what it leaves open.
### From starlight to cosmology [11] NASA Science, [‘Spectroscopy 101 – How Absorption and Emission Spectra Work’](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/science-overview/science-explainers/spectroscopy-101-how-absorption-and-emission-spectra-work/). An illustrated explanation of how astronomers identify chemical elements from light.
[12] CERN, [‘The Standard Model’](https://home.cern/science/physics/standard-model/). A guide to the particles and interactions it describes, and why gravity sits outside it.
[13] ATLAS Collaboration, CERN, [‘The Higgs boson: a landmark discovery’](https://atlas.cern/Discover/Physics/Higgs). Background on the independent ATLAS and CMS observations announced in 2012.
[14] NASA Science, [‘Big Bang and the Evolution of the Universe’](https://science.nasa.gov/astrophysics/programs/physics-of-the-cosmos/big-bang-and-the-evolution-of-the-universe/). A guide to the early universe, inflation and the cosmic microwave background.
### Quantum effects at larger scales and in technology [15] Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, [2025 Physics Nobel Prize announcement](https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2025/10/press-physicsprize2025.pdf) (7 October 2025). The award recognised experiments on tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electrical circuit; the experiments themselves date to the 1980s.
[16] Associated Press, [‘Three scientists at US universities win Nobel Prize in physics for advancing quantum technology’](https://apnews.com/article/nobel-prize-physics-e74ee2acf652259cf268cc1d48873e14) (7 October 2025). Reporting and expert context on the award, not a replication of the experiments.
[17] Pedalino and colleagues, [‘Probing quantum mechanics with nanoparticle matter-wave interferometry’](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09917-9), *Nature* (21 January 2026). The original report on interference with sodium nanoparticles.
[18] *Live Science*, [reporting on the sodium nanoparticle experiment](https://www.livescience.com/physics-mathematics/quantum-physics/physicists-push-thousands-of-atoms-to-a-schrodingers-cat-state-bringing-the-quantum-world-closer-to-reality-than-ever-before) (3 February 2026), includes an interview with lead researcher Sebastian Pedalino. It covers the same experiment as source 17.
[19] Bothwell and colleagues, [‘Resolving the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample’](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-04349-7), *Nature* (16 February 2022). A clock measurement of gravity’s effect on frequency, not a demonstration that gravity is quantum.
[20] US National Institute of Standards and Technology, [‘A Quantum Leap Forward: How Tiny Particles Can Bring Us Exciting New Tech’](https://www.nist.gov/blogs/taking-measure/quantum-leap-forward-how-tiny-particles-can-bring-us-exciting-new-tech) (18 June 2025). An accessible overview of quantum technologies.
[21] Perlin and colleagues, [‘Fault-Tolerant Execution of Error-Corrected Quantum Algorithms’](https://doi.org/10.1103/gnq3-c2df), *Physical Review X* (19 November 2026). Compares protected and unprotected circuits on trapped-ion hardware, not quantum hardware against the best conventional computer.

item.title: M&S
item.description:
Marks & Spencer wants to win more of Britain’s weekly grocery shop. This episode traces a decade of Food growth and examines what has changed behind the shelves, from bringing logistics in-house to improving stock forecasts and investing in automated distribution. It also asks what the cyberattack revealed about those efficiencies, how Food’s performance compares with fashion and Ocado Retail, and whether the shares offer good value. Figures and valuation are assessed as at 20 November 2026.
## Marks & Spencer: From the Food Hall to the Weekly Shop **Research cut-off:** 20 November 2026. **Estimated listening time:** 8 minutes.
**Key findings** - Reported Food revenue or sales rose from £5.51bn in 2015/16 to £9.72bn in 2025/26, up about 76% in nominal terms. Changes in measures, segment boundaries and reporting weeks mean this is not a like-for-like growth series. - In the half-year to September 2026, Food sales were 22.8% higher than in the equivalent pre-attack period in 2024, while operating costs rose 19.9% and gross margin was broadly flat. Adjusted operating margin rose from 5.1% to 5.6%. That supports the case for operating leverage but does not isolate the effect of individual efficiency projects. - Food’s recovery does not settle the investment question. Fashion profitability, returns on planned investment and group free cash flow also matter.
**Sources and calculation notes**
[1] Marks and Spencer Group plc, [Annual Report and Financial Statements 2016](https://corporate.marksandspencer.com/sites/marksandspencer/files/Annual%20reports/annual-report-2016.pdf). Starting-year Food revenue; the period contained 53 weeks.
[2] Marks and Spencer Group plc, [Annual Report and Financial Statements 2026](https://corporate.marksandspencer.com/sites/marksandspencer/files/marksandspencer/annual-report/m-and-s-annual-report-and-financial-statements-2026.pdf). Full-year segment results, the restated 2024/25 comparator, the impact of the cyberattack and Ocado Retail consolidation. The intermediate Food figures are drawn from M&S reporting for 2019/20, 2021/22 and 2023/24.
[3] Marks and Spencer Group plc, [Interim Results for the 26 Weeks Ended 26 September 2026](https://corporate.marksandspencer.com/sites/marksandspencer/files/2026-11/m-s-fy27-h1-rns-final.pdf), 4 November 2026. Food volume, margin and two-year operating-cost comparisons; group trading, leases and capital expenditure.
[4] Marks and Spencer Group plc, [Marks and Spencer to Acquire Gist as Part of Accelerating Its Food Supply Chain Transformation](https://corporate.marksandspencer.com/newsroom/press-releases/marks-and-spencer-acquire-gist-part-accelerating-its-food-supply-chain), July 2022. The acquisition price was an initial payment. The subsequent profit contribution is management’s assessment, not an independently measured acquisition return.
[5] Marks and Spencer Group plc, [ESG Report 2026](https://corporate.marksandspencer.com/sites/marksandspencer/files/marksandspencer/annual-report/marks-and-spencer-group-plc-esg-report-2026.pdf), June 2026. The waste figures cover wholly owned UK stores and exclude franchises, Ocado and distribution centres. The baseline is 2017/18.
[6] Financial Times, [‘M&S cyber crisis wipes almost £700mn off retailer’s valuation’](https://www.ft.com/content/1d46953a-5f2d-4395-85b9-af337a4747db), 28 April 2025. The original is paywalled; the research briefing used the Irish Times republication of the same FT report, not a second independent source. The figure refers to an early change in market capitalisation, not an operating loss.
[7] James Davey, Reuters, [‘M&S profit rebounds from cyberattack but clothing drags on recovery’](https://live.euronext.com/en/financial-news/ms-profit-rebounds-cyberattack-clothing-drags-recovery), 4 November 2026, syndicated by Euronext. Independent reporting on the contrast between the divisions.
[8] Worldpanel by Numerator, British grocery market update, 10 November 2026. The reported 14.6% growth covers grocery sales through M&S stores in the 12 weeks to 1 November. This is not directly comparable with the supermarket market-share figures in Worldpanel’s standard table.
[9] Marks and Spencer Group plc, full-year results for the 52 weeks ended 29 March 2025, Daventry investment announcement, September 2025, and [Capital Markets Day presentation transcript](https://stockanalysis.com/quote/lon/MKS/transcripts/684779-cmd-2026/), 10 November 2026. Sources for the logistics programme and management’s capacity expectations, which are not realised savings.
[10] Marks & Spencer, [‘Marks & Spencer Announces Major UAE Expansion With Launch of Biggest Foodhalls Outside of the UK’](https://corporate.marksandspencer.com/newsroom/press-releases/marks-spencer-announces-major-uae-expansion-launch-biggest-foodhalls), 2 November 2026; Target, holiday food and beverage update, 12 November 2026. Company announcements, not independent assessments of overseas demand.
[11] [London Stock Exchange: Marks and Spencer Group plc (MKS)](https://www.londonstockexchange.com/en/quote/equity/MKS/marks-and-spencer-group-plc). Valuation uses the 19 November 2026 closing price of 457.9p, not a live quote. Trailing EPS replaces the prior first half in the 2025/26 full-year figure with the latest first half: 32.0p adjusted and 25.3p statutory, implying multiples of 14.3 and 18.1 respectively. The indicated 8.4p full-year dividend implies a yield of about 1.8%. This is an editorial investment assessment, not a personal recommendation.
[12] Associated Press, [‘UK retailer Marks & Spencer puts cyberattack cost at $400 million with disruptions ongoing’](https://apnews.com/article/fef28bc0947576903cf83c3f42afc1e8), May 2025. Reporting on operational disruption; the company cost estimate covered in this article is distinct from the equity-market move reported by the Financial Times.

item.title: Mastry by Multiverse
item.description:
Can an AI coach teach employees a skill they can still use once the coach is gone? This buyer’s review traces Multiverse’s evolution from apprenticeships to enterprise software, examines what is publicly known about Mastry’s architecture, and compares it with Section, Microsoft Copilot and other alternatives. Early feedback suggests the diagnostic can uncover barriers to adoption, but it does not prove that coaching improves skills. We explain what to verify before sharing workplace data and how to run a pilot that distinguishes faster output from lasting learning.
# Mastry by Multiverse: Can an AI coach teach people to work differently? **Runtime:** Approximately 10–11 minutes. **Evidence cut-off:** 20 November 2026.
**Buyer verdict:** Shortlist for a controlled pilot, not a workforce-wide rollout. Mastry’s proposition is to link diagnosis, coaching on live tasks and evidence of applied skill. The pilot should test what Mastry adds over an existing AI assistant and whether employees can apply what they learnt on a different task without Mae.
## Sources and what they establish - **Product and availability:** Multiverse’s [launch announcement](https://www.multiverse.io/blog/multiverse-launches-mastry-single-platform-ai-ambition-ai-adoption) (14 October 2026) describes the three-stage flow. Eligible development partners could join a waitlist at the research cut-off; full launch was planned for early 2027, not confirmed. Its [Workforce 2030 recap](https://www.multiverse.io/blog/workforce-2030-key-takeaways) (30 October 2026) is the source for the meeting-preparation demonstration and Sarah Gallo’s account of the News UK diagnostic pilot. Neither establishes full-product outcomes. - **Technical architecture:** Multiverse’s [diagnostic overview](https://www.multiverse.io/blog/leaders-precise-insights-every-department-ai-capability-adoption-barriers) (12 October 2026) describes the inputs and reporting. The [AI Engineering Manager vacancy](https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/multiverse/9cd634af-ef58-4f76-8c41-06ef5e87d02c) describes retrieval, assessment scoring and a move towards dedicated services in the broader engineering estate, not a verified Mastry stack. ‘Meet the minds behind Mastry: Inside Multiverse’s AI engineering team’ (20 November 2026) identifies the team but does not provide a deployment diagram. The product-specific Trust Centre FAQs were listed but their contents were not verified. - **Company and training:** [Index Ventures’ Multiverse profile](https://www.indexventures.com/companies/whitehat/) provides investor context. Ufi VocTech Trust covered the WhiteHat rebrand (26 January 2021); TechCrunch reported on the Series D (8 June 2022) and Searchlight purchase (8 April 2024). Multiverse announced StackFuel on 27 January 2026 and its funding round on 15 May 2026. Its [Atlas coaching announcement](https://www.multiverse.io/blog/launching-on-demand-coaching-powered-by-ai) and [2026 Impact Report announcement](https://www.multiverse.io/blog/announcing-our-2026-impact-report) concern the training business. [Ofsted’s inspection report](https://reports.ofsted.gov.uk/provider/33/1276443) (published 21 May 2026) supplies an independent view; the company set out its response in ‘Understanding Multiverse completion rates — and why context matters’ (20 May 2026). - **Competitive alternatives:** [Section’s AI Proficiency Assessment](https://proficiencytest.sectionai.com/), Section Coach and Section HQ offer the closest functional comparison. Microsoft Learn’s Copilot release notes (27 October 2026) and Copilot Dashboard documentation describe a native alternative for Microsoft-centred buyers. WalkMe’s technical overview and Accenture’s ‘Accenture Invests in Workhelix to Help Organizations Prepare their Workforces for Generative AI’ address adjacent workflow and transformation needs. These are supplier descriptions, not comparative benchmarks. - **Launch coverage and demand:** Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin’s CMOtech coverage (27 October 2026) also ran on IT Brief; that is not separate corroboration. Sam Allcock covered the launch in Daily Tech Times (9 November 2026). Neither outlet independently tested the product. The UK government’s [AI adoption survey 2026](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-adoption-survey-2026) (29 October 2026) documents the broader skills barrier, not demand for Mastry.
**Before piloting:** Request host-specific permissions, data flows, retention rules, hosting and isolation details, and clarity on who can see individual evidence. Keep pilot data out of performance management. Compare quality-adjusted time and independent task performance against existing tools and training, then account for licensing, coaching and staff time.

item.title: New Serbian Government
item.description:
Serbia’s Student List won an outright parliamentary majority in October 2026, ending fourteen years of dominance by the Serbian Progressive Party. Yet as of 20 November, the old cabinet was still in office as caretaker. This episode explains how a movement organised through campus assemblies won control of parliament, what the constitution requires before it can govern, and what Nepal, Chile and Thailand reveal about the difference between winning an election and taking office.
## New Serbian Government
**Reporting cut-off:** 20 November 2026. Serbia’s Student List won 140 of 250 parliamentary seats; the Serbian Progressive Party-led United Serbia list won 103. The vote changed control of the Assembly, but a new cabinet had yet to be elected. The episode compares three different routes from political mobilisation to office: a lower-house majority in Nepal, a presidential victory without a congressional majority in Chile, and a parliamentary plurality constrained by an appointed Senate in Thailand.
### Serbia: result, transition and constitutional rules
1. Republic Electoral Commission of Serbia, [*Ukupan izveštaj o rezultatima izbora za narodne poslanike Narodne skupštine*](https://www.rik.parlament.gov.rs/extfile/sr/files/additionalDocuments/822/431/Ukupan%20izve%C5%A1taj%20o%20rezultatima%20izbora%20za%20narodne%20poslanike%20Narodne%20skup%C5%A1tine.pdf), 5 November 2026. Official final results, in Serbian. 2. Radio Television of Serbia, [*RIK proglasio konačne rezultate izbora: Studentska lista 140, Ujedinjena Srbija 103 mandata*](https://www.rts.rs/lat/vesti/izbori-2026/6077524/rik-proglasio-konacne-rezultate-izbora.html), 5 November 2026. Serbian-language coverage of the commission’s announcement, not an independent count. 3. National Assembly of Serbia, [*Prva sednica Narodne skupštine Republike Srbije u Petnaestom sazivu*](https://www.parlament.gov.rs/Prva_sednica_Narodne_skupstine_Republike_Srbije_u_Petnaestom_sazivu.54099.941.html), 17–19 November 2026. Official record of the opening sitting and speaker’s election, in Serbian. 4. Jovana Gec, Associated Press, [*University lecturer from Serbia’s student-led movement is elected Parliament speaker*](https://apnews.com/article/serbia-parliament-speaker-students-380e56549eca2c3190f5d1809194a0a2), 19 November 2026. Reporting on the speaker’s election, Vučić’s resignation and the pending cabinet vote. 5. BizSrbija, [*Srbija ima Skupštinu i v.d. predsednika Republike, čeka se Vlada i budžet*](https://bizsrbija.rs/artikal/srbija-ima-skupstinu-i-v-d-predsednika-ceka-se-vlada-i-budzet), 20 November 2026. Serbian-language coverage of the cabinet vote still to come. 6. Constitutional Court of Serbia, [*Ustav Republike Srbije*](https://www.ustavni.sud.rs/ustav-rs-i-propisi/ustav-republike-srbije?lang_type=lat). The Serbian constitution; see Articles 109, 120, 127 and 128 on government formation, the acting presidency, the cabinet vote and caretaker powers.
### How the movement organised and what it promised
7. OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and partner observer delegations, [*Serbia, Early Parliamentary Elections, 25 October 2026: Statement of Preliminary Findings and Conclusions*](https://odihr.osce.org/odihr/669165), 26 October 2026. Preliminary observation of turnout, competition and unequal campaign conditions. 8. Branislav Jakovljević and Danica Pajović, *TDR*, [*Performing the Political Unknown: A Report on the Student Protest Movement in Serbia*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/the-drama-review/article/performing-the-political-unknown/A815A21EC0CA2E3AE8C256A6BC3FC6D6), 22 June 2026. Academic account of the campus plenums and their decision-making. 9. UK House of Commons Library, [*Serbia under Aleksandar Vučić and the 2026 parliamentary election*](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-12267/). Parliamentary research briefing on the protest movement, the Student List and the election. 10. CRTA / Otvoreni parlament, [*Aleksandar Čupić izabran za predsednika Skupštine, preuzima dužnost predsednika Republike*](https://crta.plus/sr/updates/aleksandar-cupic-izabran-za-predsednika-skupstine/), 20 November 2026. Serbian parliamentary watchdog account of the leadership votes, opposition objections and previous practice.
### International comparisons
11. Inter-Parliamentary Union, Parline, [*Nepal House of Representatives March 2026 Election*](https://data.ipu.org/parliament/NP/NP-LC01/election/NP-LC01-E20260305/), election held 5 March 2026. Results and transition to office. 12. Madhav Joshi, *Journal of World Affairs*, [*Nepal’s Parliamentary Election After the Gen-Z Movement: Ten Observations on a Political Change in the Making*](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/29769442261483366), 13 September 2026. Scholarly commentary distinguishing the protest movement from the party that won the election. 13. Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional de Chile, [*Reseña biográfica: Gabriel Boric Font*](https://www.bcn.cl/historiapolitica/resenas_parlamentarias/wiki/Gabriel_Boric_Font). Spanish-language parliamentary biography covering Boric’s student activism, congressional career and presidential election. 14. Claudia Zilla, German Institute for International and Security Affairs, [*Gabriel Boric Assumes Office in Chile*](https://www.swp-berlin.org/10.18449/2022C18/), 9 March 2022. Analysis of Boric’s coalition and the absence of a governing majority in Congress. 15. Gregory V. Raymond, *Journal of Current Southeast Asian Affairs*, [*Authoritarian Securitisation and Moral Panic: The Discourse and Role of the Senate in the 2023 Thai Election*](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/18681034251320658), 24 February 2025. Academic analysis of the appointed Senate’s role under the rules in force in 2023.
### Campaign programme
16. Studentska lista — Studenti pobeđuju, [*Program: Studentski plan*](https://gg.studenti.org.rs/studentski-plan.pdf), 2026 election campaign. The movement’s Serbian-language platform documents its commitments; it does not establish that they have been implemented.

item.title: Global Concrete usage
item.description:
How much concrete does the world use, and when is it worth the cost? This episode compares ready-mix and cement figures from China, India, Vietnam, the United States and Türkiye, explaining why production figures aren’t a measure of domestic use. From kiln emissions to sand dredging in the Mekong Delta, it weighs concrete’s environmental costs against the reasons engineers still rely on it for bridges, foundations and water infrastructure.
## How to read the numbers Ready-mix figures cover only part of the concrete market, and the country examples are from different years. Cement production is a separate measure: it includes material destined for products such as mortar and does not account for where traded cement is ultimately used. The episode’s emissions total covers direct cement-making emissions from chemical reactions and kiln fuels, not the full concrete supply chain.
## Sources [1] Takuma Watari and colleagues, iScience, [‘Growing role of concrete in sand and climate crises’](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10214720/) (2023). Peer-reviewed estimate of global concrete and mortar production in 2020.
[2] China Concrete and Cement Products Association, [‘Ready-Mixed Concrete Industry Development Report of the Year 2025’](https://en.chinaconcrete.com.cn/cnt_517.html); US National Ready Mixed Concrete Association, ‘Estimated Ready Mixed Concrete Production By State – 2024’; Turkish Ready Mixed Concrete Association, ‘Türkiye Hazır Beton Sektörü İstatistikleri – 2024’, drawing on European Ready Mixed Concrete Organisation data. The US estimate is rounded after conversion from cubic yards.
[3] US Geological Survey, [‘Cement’, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026](https://pubs.usgs.gov/periodicals/mcs2026/mcs2026.pdf) (2026); Vietnam Ministry of Industry and Trade, ‘Overview Report on Vietnam’s Domestic Market 2025’, for the domestic cement consumption estimate.
[4] Robbie Andrew, [‘Global CO₂ emissions from cement production’](https://zenodo.org/records/22178444) (2026 data release). The process and fossil-fuel estimates are rounded separately.
[5] UN Environment Programme, [‘Sand and Sustainability: 10 Strategic Recommendations to Avert a Crisis’](https://wedocs.unep.org/items/9ec225c4-5a9f-44d0-a560-46e0c8264003) (2022). Covers erosion, habitat damage and other consequences of sand extraction.
[6] WWF and partners, ‘Sand Budget for Viet Nam Mekong Delta’ (August 2023); Brice Pedroletti and Adrienne Surprenant, Le Monde, ‘Water rises and land sinks in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta’ (1 November 2025). Le Monde cites the sand budget for the extraction figures and adds field reporting on the delta’s sediment shortage; it is not a second estimate of extraction.
[7] Sabbie Miller, Arpad Horvath and Paulo Monteiro, Nature Sustainability, [‘Impacts of booming concrete production on water resources worldwide’](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41893-017-0009-5) (2018). The water figure refers to estimated industrial withdrawals in 2012, not current withdrawals or all global water use.
[8] Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, [‘Industry’, Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group III](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/chapter/chapter-11/) (2022). Cement chemistry, material efficiency and industrial decarbonisation options.
[9] UN Environment Programme and Yale Center for Ecosystems + Architecture, [‘Building Materials and the Climate: Constructing a New Future’](https://www.unep.org/pt-br/node/35039) (2023). A framework for avoiding unnecessary new material, shifting to suitable alternatives and improving conventional materials.
[10] Associated Press, [‘LA fires charred homes into piles of metal and concrete. By recycling them, they’re given new life’](https://apnews.com/article/la-fires-eaton-fire-steel-concrete-trees-recycling-rebuilding-b40594fef233399c4c9e1fe62a83aa85) (18 July 2025). A reported example of demolition concrete being recovered for reuse.
